1.48.m: Brahmā said: / But after this, O brahmin-sage, a twice-born fallen to an outcaste state, / lamenting with many sorrows, went to the sage Kaśyapa.
Having gone, he said: 'O best of sages, speak words beneficial to me; / act so that I may be freed from sin, O best of sages!'
The one of great splendor, smiling slightly, said to him from all sides; / Kaśyapa said: 'Even from the sight of barbarians, you yourself have indeed been subdued.
Through recitations of the Gāyatrī, oblations into the fire, and vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, / continually remembering the foot of Hari, fasting on Hari's day,
meditating day and night on Hari, bow down to that Lord. / By bathing at sacred places with mantras, you will reach the end of [your] mire.
Then, solely through the destruction of sin, you will regain the status of a brahmin, / destroying your stain through vows superior in merit, [attaining] liberation, O twice-born.'
Hearing that sage's speech, he then considered his purpose achieved; / having performed diverse merits, he regained the status of a brahmin.
Then, having performed severe austerities, he went to heaven for a long time. / The entire sin of a person of virtuous conduct diminishes day by day;
the merit of a person of bad conduct indeed diminishes like collyrium. / A twice-born is ruined by improper conduct, [but] through proper conduct he reaches divinity.
Therefore, even with breath in his throat, a twice-born practices proper conduct; / with action, mind, and body, always practice good conduct.
By the instruction of Kaśyapa, that twice-born became disciplined; / having again practiced proper conduct and performed austerities, he went to heaven.
A twice-born devoid of proper conduct is ruined, reviled in heavenly worlds; / but having again practiced proper conduct, he is honored in the world of the gods.
Nārada said: / People attain a good state by honoring the best of the twice-born. / By oppressing the twice-born, to what state does one go, O Lord?
Brahmā said: / A man who does not honor according to his capacity and with devotion / the high-souled brahmins whose bodies are tormented by hunger goes to hell.
Whoever, having reviled [one] harshly, dismisses him in anger, / goes to the terrible hell, the harsh Mahāraurava.
Having returned from there, he is born among lowest castes from an insect [state]; / then he is diseased, poor, and tormented by hunger.
Therefore, one should not insult a twice-born who has come to one's house hungry. / Whoever says, 'I will not give,' toward gods, fires, and brahmins,
having passed through a hundred wombs of beasts, goes to an outcaste state. / Whoever raises a foot and strikes a twice-born, a cow, parents, or a guru,
his dwelling in Raurava is fixed; there is no expiation for him here. / If by merit he should gain birth, he becomes a cripple,
exceedingly wretched and sorrowful, tormented by grief and suffering. / Thus having experienced three births, his expiation occurs.
A man who strikes a twice-born with fists, slaps, or blows, / dwells in Tāpana and terrible Raurava until the end of the kalpa.
Then, obtaining a birth, he becomes a cruel, fierce dog, / or born among the lowest castes, poor and afflicted with belly-ache.
Or whoever raises a foot [against a brahmin], elephantiasis appears in his foot, / or a man becomes lame, or slow in his shanks, or has a maimed foot;
and his limbs tremble constantly with hemiplegia. / Having killed mother, father, a twice-born, a snātaka, an ascetic,
or a group of teachers in anger, he remains in Kumbhīpāka for a long time; / and having dwelt [there], he is born after that in the species of worms.
Whoever speaks hostile, harsh words to the twice-born, / eight kinds of leprosy certainly arise in his body, O son:
scabies, then ringworm, circular leprosy, oyster-shell leprosy, and white leprosy, / black leprosy, white leprosy, and juvenile leprosy, which is exceedingly severe.
Then, despite a physician's treatment, merit flees because of the sin; / like a line drawn in water, because of demerit he goes to death through that very thing.
Among these, only three are proclaimed as major leprosies: / black leprosy, white leprosy, and juvenile leprosy, which is exceedingly severe.
Through the state of great sins, through knowledge, or through association, / the three certainly arise in the bodies of the greatest sinners.
Disease spreads among men from contact, from association. / A wise man should avoid them from afar; if he touches [one], he should perform a bath.
Having touched a fallen person, a leper, an outcaste, a beef-eater, / a dog, a menstruating woman, or a Bhilla, one should perform a bath.
Leprosies are settled in the body in accordance with one's sin, / both in this world and in the next; there is no doubt about this.
Whoever takes away a brahmin's property, a livelihood acquired rightfully, / goes to an imperishable hell; there is no rebirth [for him].
Whoever is a slanderer of twice-borns, intent on seeking out their faults— / seeing or touching him, one should enter water with one's clothes on.
A brahmin's property enjoyed out of affection burns the family up to the seventh [generation]; / but enjoying it by force, [it burns] ten ancestors and ten descendants.
They say that poison is not [true] poison; a brahmin's property is called poison: / poison kills only a single person, [but] a brahmin's property kills sons and grandsons.
Having approached one's mother out of delusion, or a brāhmaṇī, or the wife of a guru, / falling into terrible Raurava, another birth is difficult to obtain.
His ancestors fall into Kumbhīpāka, into Tāpana, / into Avīci, Kālasūtra, and Mahāraurava and Raurava.
They never allow any expiation for them. / Having destroyed the life of the twice-born, one goes personally to [a state of] non-rebirth [in heaven],
and his ancestors fall into Raurava by the thousands. / Nārada said: 'Is the sin equal in the killing of all twice-borns,
or where would a difference lie? You should explain this according to the truth.' / Brahmā said: 'Having killed a twice-born, O son, the sin is declared as fixed;
the slayer of a brahmin incurs a terrible [sin]. Hear another matter to be spoken: / he incurs the sin of killing a hundred thousand, a crore, a thousand brahmins,
if he kills a master of the Veda endowed with the Vedas and scriptures, whose senses are conquered; / and having killed a twice-born who is a Vaiṣṇava, ten times greater than that.
Having caused his lineages to fall, he does not find another [good] birth; / having killed a snātaka of three Vedas, he finds no end to his slaughter.
For the slayer of a master of the Veda of good conduct, purified by sacred places and mantras— / for the slayer of such a brahmin, there is no end to his sin.
If a twice-born gives up his life on account of a wrong done [to him], / that other person by whom he is seen becomes a slayer of a brahmin.
A twice-born oppressed and beaten with harsh words and actions, / on account of whom he gives up his life—they call that man a slayer of a brahmin.'

Sages, ascetics, gods, and all knowers of Brahman,
and rulers of countries—such a person is to be slain here in this world.

Therefore, incurring [the guilt of] slaying a brāhmaṇa, he is cooked [in hell] along with his ancestors.
A wise man must certainly honor a vipra who undertakes fasting unto death.

If one should surrender his life pointing to someone entirely free from faults,
he is smeared with dreadful slaughters, but not he whom he proclaims.

One who commits suicide, climbing a tree, or one living off hollows,
he who slays himself becomes a slayer of a brāhmaṇa within his own lineage.

And he who destroys an embryo, an infant, an afflicted person, or a guru,
is himself a slayer of a brāhmaṇa; but not he whom he proclaims.

Or if the basest of brāhmaṇas slays a member of the same gotra or a brāhmaṇa,
that sin belongs solely to him, and not to him whom he proclaims.

A śūdra who tortures a twice-born to accomplish his own purpose,
in that sinless [victim], the sin of the śūdra definitely remains unabated.

By slaying at once an assailant who kills,
O best of the twice-born, the slayer is not tainted with sins.

Even if an assailant who approaches is a master of the Vedānta, in battle,
if one desires to kill him who desires to kill, one does not become a slayer of a brāhmaṇa thereby.

An incendiary, a poisoner, a thief of wealth, a slayer of those asleep,
a stealer of land, and a stealer of wives: these six are indeed assailants.

A rogue, one attempting to assassinate a king, one intent on killing ancestors,
and an invading king against a king: these four are also assailants.

If a vipra does not die instantly, it is not proper to strike him again.
Having struck him again knowingly, one certainly incurs the terrible guilt of murder.

There is no one equal to a vipra in the world; he is a guru of the universe, worthy of worship.
Whatever sin arises from slaying him, there is nothing beyond that.

He should be worshipped like a god by hosts of gods, asuras, and mortals.
There is certainly no equal to a brāhmaṇa in the three worlds.

Nārada said:
Resorting to what livelihood should a twice-born live
in distress, O best of the gods? You should tell me according to truth.

relying upon which the best of munis go to the realm of Brahman.
The sacrificial fee from remnants of sacrifice should indeed be accepted by one engaged in sacrifice.

Twice-borns should accept wealth by teaching and by officiating at sacrifices,
and after teaching, studying, and performing auspicious rites of benediction.

This is the livelihood of brāhmaṇas; acceptance of gifts is the livelihood of the upright.
Fortunate are those who live off sacred texts; fortunate are those who live off trees;

fortunate are those whose livelihood comes from trees and creepers, and those who live off gardens and crops.
For the expiation of the sin of killing insects in the food,

one should cause new, praised grains to be given to vipras;
otherwise, through the killing of living beings here, one’s lifespan will surely decline.

Therefore, one should give bountifully to ancestors, gods, and the twice-born.
In the absence [of other means], the kṣatriya livelihood is adopted by brāhmaṇas.

One should fight in righteous wars, observing the auspicious vow of a hero.
Whatever wealth a twice-born obtains from a king by that livelihood,

that wealth is declared pure for offerings to ancestors and for gifts.
The sinless one should always practice the science of archery united with the Vedas,

along with javelins, spears, maces, swords, and iron clubs all around,
horse-riding, elephant-riding, illusions, and measures,

and should engage appropriately everywhere in combat on chariots and on ground.
For the protection of twice-borns, gods, the steadfast, women, ascetics,

the virtuous, virtuous women, gurus, and kings,
whatever merit is obtained by heroes, how could it [not] be obtained by teachers of the Veda?

Having destroyed all sins, he enjoys imperishable heaven.
Brāhmaṇas who fall face-forward in righteous war,

reach the supreme realm, inaccessible even to teachers of the Veda.
Hear accurately the merit and conduct of righteous warfare:

They fight face to face and do not become cowardly;
they do not strike a broken foe from behind, nor one unarmed, nor one fleeing,

nor one not fighting, nor a coward, nor one fallen, nor one free of taint,
nor a base śūdra, nor one pleasing with praise, nor one who has sought refuge in battle.

Slaying [such people], evil-minded men seeking victory go to hell.
And this kṣatriya livelihood is praised by good conduct,

relying upon which all preeminent kṣatriyas go to heaven.
Auspicious is the death of a kṣatriya facing the front in righteous battle.

There he becomes purified and is freed from all sins.
He dwells in the heavenly world in a palace adorned with jewels,

with pillars made of gold, with floors adorned with jewels,
filled with desirable objects, and decorated with celestial fabrics.

Before him stand wish-fulfilling trees, bestowing everything,
[in grounds] adorned with stepwells, wells, ponds, and gardens.

Maidens of the celestial city, endowed with youth, attend him;
troops of apsarases dance perpetually with joy before him.

Gandharvas sing songs, and gods recite eulogies.
In this manner, at the end of a kalpa, he becomes a sovereign king,

the sole enjoyer of all pleasures, free from disease, the very embodiment of Kāma.
His wives are endowed with supreme beauty, continually possessing youth.

His sons are righteous, splendid, prosperous, and pleasing to their ancestors.
In this sequence, good kṣatriyas enjoy [such fruits] for seven births.

Those who fight unrighteously, however, remain in hell for a long time.
Thus, the kṣatriya livelihood is also practiced by brāhmaṇas,

and by vaiśyas, śūdras, and others, outcastes, and mleccha classes;
those warriors who fight always in righteous war,

they too go to the supreme realm, along with all castes and the twice-born.
A twice-born who is not heroic, but cowardly and devoid of weapons,

the best of twice-born may cause to adopt the vaiśya livelihood in misfortune:
the vaiśya livelihood, the merchant’s occupation, and agriculture through others.

He may cause agriculture and trade to be carried out; a brāhmaṇa must not abandon his duties. / If he speaks falsely through the disposition of a merchant, the twice-born would attain misfortune.

By avoiding wet merchandise, a brāhmaṇa attains well-being.
Having generated a livelihood from that, he should give to a vipra in every way.

In the ancestral sacrifice and in the fire, a twice-born should offer according to rule.
Dishonesty must not be practiced at the scale, for the scale is established on dharma.

Practicing deceit on the balance, one goes to hell;
and even with goods not weighed, one should cast aside deceit.

Thus falsehood should not be practiced; untruth gives birth to sin.
There is no dharma higher than truth; there is no greater sin than falsehood.

Therefore, in all undertakings, truth alone is superior.
A thousand horse sacrifices and truth were weighed on a scale;

indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse sacrifices.
He who speaks truth in all matters and renounces falsehood,

crosses over difficulties and enjoys imperishable heaven.
A vipra may engage in trade, but he must necessarily abandon falsehood.

And he should deposit the profit at a sacred ford and personally consume only the remainder;
owing to bodily exertion, that becomes a thousandfold greater at all times.

In the process of acquiring wealth, mortals plunge into treacherous waters,
and into the wilderness and forest infested with predatory beasts.
To a mountain, an inaccessible mountain cave, the house of sword-wielding barbarians, / and a terrifying place, [they go] on all sides out of greed for wealth.
Abandoning their sons and wives, the greedy go far away; / others bear burdens on their shoulders, [thrown] on a boat or thrown down by the wheel,
by means of oars, amid great sufferings, and with perpetual expenditure of life. / The accumulation of great wealth, O son, is dearer than life.
Wealth earned justly by these means, with effort, in the manner of a merchant, / when given to ancestors, gods, and twice-born, attains imperishable [reward].
There are two great faults in trade, in the pursuit of profit: / failure to relinquish greed, and falsely taking goods for sale.
A wise man, abandoning these two faults, should earn wealth; / he obtains an imperishable [fruit] through giving, and is not tainted by the merchant's faults.
A brāhmaṇa devoted to virtuous deeds should indeed have farming done: / he should have four oxen yoked for half a day,
or three if they are lacking, and he must not cause them to work without rest. / He should graze them on uncut grass free of thieves and tigers.
He should give fodder as desired, and always satisfy [them] himself. / He should make a cowpen for them free of any trouble,
always free of cow dung, urine, and scraps of food. / One should not throw filth in a cowpen, the abode of all the gods.
The wise man should make it equal to his own bed; / he should carefully ward off cold, wind, and dust equally.
He should look upon a cow as equal to his own life, sharing a common form: / the pleasure or pain in its body is reckoned just as in his own.
Whoever causes agricultural work to be done according to this rule / is not tainted by the sins of driving cattle, and will become wealthy.
Whoever afflicts a weak [beast], or one afflicted with illness, / or one too young or too old, incurs [the sin of] cow-slaughter.
Whoever yokes unequally—a weak beast with a strong one— / incurs a sin equal to cow-slaughter in this world, without a doubt.
Whoever drives [cattle] without grain, or holds back an eating cow / from grass or water out of delusion, incurs [a sin] equal to cow-slaughter.
On the passage of the sun into a zodiac sign, on a full moon day, and likewise on a new moon day, / the sin from driving a plow is equal to the slaughter of ten thousand cows.
A person who worships these [cows] on those [days] with white and varicolored [garments], / with collyrium, flowers, and oils, attains imperishable heaven.
Whoever gives a handful of grass to another's cow as a daily duty, / for him there is destruction of all sins, and he enjoys imperishable heaven.
As is a brāhmaṇa, so is a cow: the fruit of worshiping either is the same. / In consideration, the brāhmaṇa is foremost among men, and likewise cows among animals.
Nārada said: / 'The brāhmaṇa was born from Brahmā's mouth'—thus it was told by you to me, O sinless one. / How is he equal to cows, O Lord? Indeed, wonder arises in me, O Ordainer!
Brahmā said: / Listen here to the truth regarding brāhmaṇas and cows, / how their unity as a single mass was fashioned of old by the Supreme Being.
Formerly, from the mouth of Brahmā, a great, radiant mass arose; / it became divided into four parts: the Veda, fire, the cow, and the twice-born.
The first to arise from that radiance was the Veda, and likewise fire; / next, the cow and the brāhmaṇa were born separately.
There, the four Vedas were created by me first, one by one, / for the maintenance of all worlds and realms on every side.
Fire eats the sacrificial offerings, and so does the twice-born for the sake of the gods. / Know that clarified butter arises from the cow; therefore these were produced.
If these four eminent ones were not present in the worlds, / then the entire world, stationary and moving, would be destroyed.
Upheld by these, the worlds always endure by nature; / that nature is the form of Brahman, and these are remembered as composed of Brahman.
Therefore this cow is to be worshiped even by brāhmaṇas, gods, and asuras; / it is generous in all actions, born true, a mine of virtues,
manifestly composed of all the gods, compassionate to all beings. / Its function in sustaining [the world] was created by me long ago.
For this very reason, a most auspicious boon was given by me: / 'In a single birth your liberation is assured!'
The cows that die here go to my abode; / not a particle of sin remains in their body.
The cow is a goddess, the milch cow of the gods, the primordial goddess possessing threefold power; / by her grace the source of sacrifices is indeed established.
All the pure substances of cows purify the entire world: / the urine of the cow, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter.
When these are eaten, no sin remains in the body; / therefore the righteous continually consume clarified butter, curd, and milk.
Produce of the cow is distinguished among all substances, desirable, and supremely auspicious; / the body of him in whose mouth it is absent becomes putrid.
Grains and the like [last] for five nights, milk indeed for seven nights, / curd for twenty nights, and clarified butter can last for one month.
Whoever eats food devoid of cow-products for a full month continuously— / in that mortal's meal spirits of the dead indeed eat.
Having eaten the supremely pure sweet rice cooked with sun-dried rice grains, / whatever merit is performed becomes multiplied tens of millions of times.
Moreover, whatever other offering-food is prescribed by the scriptures, / whatever deed is performed after eating that becomes multiplied a hundred thousand times.
Whatever vegetarian food [is eaten], whatever fruit is obtained from it— / therefore the cow alone is praised in all actions, age after age.
She always grants dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation in all desires. / Nārada said: / In what matters or by what practice is supreme merit proclaimed?
Speak that, O Lord of all the worlds, that I may know it truly. / Brahmā said: / Having circumambulated even once, one should bow to the herd of cows.
Completely freed from all sins, he attains imperishable heaven. / Just as the preceptor of the gods is to be revered, just as Mādhava is to be worshiped,
[and] just as Indra [attained] dominion after performing seven circumambulations; / rising at dawn in the midst of cows, holding a vessel with water,
whoever sprinkles the horns of the cows and receives that water on his head / while fasting—learn of his merit!
Whatever sacred pilgrimage places are heard of in the three worlds, O Nārada, / accompanied by Siddhas and Cāraṇas and frequented by great sages,
the bathing in all of them is [attained] by the water from the horns of cows. / Rising early in the morning, whichever mortal touches a cow, clarified butter, honey,
mustard seeds, and priyaṅgu seeds is freed from sin. / 'Cows grant clarified butter and milk; cows are the womb of clarified butter, born of clarified butter;
cows are rivers of clarified butter, whirlpools of clarified butter; may they always be in my house! / Clarified butter is in all my limbs; clarified butter is situated in my mind.
Cows are always in front of me, and cows are behind me; / cows are in all my limbs; I dwell in the midst of cows.'
Having thus sipped water, pure, he should recite this mantra evening and morning; / all his sins are destroyed, and he becomes honored in the heavenly world.
As is a cow, so is a brāhmaṇa; as is a brāhmaṇa, so is Hari; / as is Hari, so is the Gaṅgā: these are remembered as never unyielding.
Cows are the kin of men, and men are the kinsmen of cows; / and in whichever house there is no cow, that house is devoid of kin.
The Vedas, together with the six auxiliary limbs and the pada and krama recitations, reside in the mouth of the cow; / and upon her two horns dwell Hari and Keśava constantly together.
Skanda is situated in her belly, Brahmā ever resides in her head, / the bull-bannered [Śiva] is on her forehead, and Indra on the tips of her horns.
The two divine Aśvins are in her ears, the moon and sun in her eyes, / the god Garuḍa is in her teeth, and Sarasvatī on her tongue.
All holy bathing places are in her anus, and the Jāhnavī [Gaṅgā] is in her urine; / the sages reside in the pores of her hair, [while] in front and at the back is Yama.
Kubera and Varuṇa reside on her right side; / on the left side are stationed the Yakṣas, radiant and mighty.
The Gandharvas reside in the middle of her mouth, and the serpents at the tip of her nose; / while on the back part of her hooves the Apsarases reside.
Lakṣmī dwells in cow dung, and Sarvamaṅgalā in cow urine; / the sky-dwellers are to be known at the tips of her feet, and Prajāpati in her lowing sound.
The four full oceans verily reside in the teats of cows; / and he who touches a cow daily becomes ever cleansed by bathing.
Therefore, a mortal is freed from all sins by those [cows] well nurtured; / and he who carries on his head the dust raised by the hooves of cows,

has bathed in the waters of holy places and is freed from all sins.
Nārada said: / What is the fruit of giving which [cow] among the ten colors of cows?

Tell the truth, O best of gurus, O Parameṣṭhin, if it is pleasing [to you].
Brahmā said: / Having given a white cow to a Brahmin, a man becomes a lord;
He ever lives in a mansion, enjoying pleasures and flourishing in happiness. / A smoke-colored [cow] liberates from sin in the round of rebirth, [like] a wilderness of heaven;
The gift of a reddish-brown cow brings inexhaustible [merit]; having given a black [cow], one does not suffer; / a pale-white one is rare in the world, and a fair one gladdens the family.
A red-eyed [cow] is for one desiring beauty, and a dark-blue one is for one desiring wealth; / having given a single reddish-brown cow, one is freed from all sins.
Whatever sin is committed in childhood, committed in youth or in old age, / committed by speech, committed by deed, or mentally pondered;
Approaching an improper woman, the sin of betraying a friend, / false weights, false balances, falsehood concerning a maiden, or falsehood concerning a cow—
he who gives a reddish-brown cow swiftly destroys all of that. / [When facing] the great river Mahāpārā, ten leagues wide,
in an ocean of water rushing across a wilderness of water with iron arrows [as waves]— / as long as the two feet and the head of the calf have not yet emerged,
so long is the cow to be known as the Earth, while she has not yet discharged the fetus. / [One should give a cow] with golden horns, adorned with garments, decorated with all ornaments,
with a copper-plated back, silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel, / adorned with fragrant scents and flowers, and embellished with all ornaments.
One should give such a reddish-brown cow to a twice-born who has mastered the Vedas; / his sins are all destroyed, and he becomes unfailing in the world of Viṣṇu.
While she is being milked, the drops that fall upon the ground / turn into gardens and the like, excellent with abundant flowers and fruits.
Where trees yield desired fruits, rivers have mud of sweet milk-rice, / and mansions are golden—there go the givers of cows.
He who gives ten cows and one draft bull / is said to obtain equal fruit; this has been proclaimed by Brahmā.
One gives one [bull] with ten [cows]—the fruit is a hundred thousand [cows]. / In accordance with that, O Nārada, the fruit is to be known with effort.
The son who releases a bull on earth for the sake of the ancestors / causes the ancestors to be honored in the worlds of Viṣṇu as they desire.
And four heifers are to be released / for one bull alone on all sides, O son; this is the eternal rule.
For as many hairs as there are on it and on all of them, / for so many thousands of years mortals enjoy heaven.
The water that a bull certainly scatters with his tail / becomes nectar for the ancestors for a thousand years.
With his hoof he plows the earth, and from it arises a clod and mud; / the svadhā offering there for the ancestors becomes a hundred thousand crores of times [more fruitful].
If a mother dies while the father is still living, / a cow marked with sandalwood is given for her attainment of heaven.
The giver is truly freed from debt to the ancestors; / he attains imperishable heaven, honored like Maghavan.
A young cow endowed with all auspicious marks, rich in milk, / delivered at the proper time, auspicious—that cow is regarded as the earth.
By the gift of it with the mantra, the fruit is equal to the gift of the earth; / a mortal equal to Śatakratu delivers a hundred lineages.
Having stolen cows, when a bull or a calf has died, / one would stay in a well full of worms until the dissolution of all beings.
And having slaughtered cows, one is cooked along with one's ancestors / in the dreadful Raurava hell; for such a time is the retribution.
One who breaks up a cow-pasture, or yokes and binds a castrated bull, / would enter an imperishable hell, again in birth after birth.
Whoever recites even once this most meritorious story, / for him there is the destruction of all sins, and he rejoices with the gods.
Or whoever listens to this supreme, most meritorious, great [narrative] / is at that very moment freed from sin committed over seven lifetimes.

1.49.m: Nārada said: / By what conduct does the brahmanical radiance of a vipra increase? / By what conduct does that same brahmanical radiance perish?
Brahmā said: / Having arisen from his bed in the last portion of the night, the best of twice-borns / should always and certainly remember the gods, as well as the meritorious ones:
Govinda, Mādhava, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, and Dāmodara; / Nārāyaṇa, Jagannātha, Vāsudeva, the unborn, all-pervading Lord;
Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas; / Brahmā, the Sun, the Moon, the guardians of the directions, and the planets;
Śaṅkara, Śiva, Śambhu, Īśvara, and Maheśvara; / Gaṇeśa, Skanda, Gaurī, and the auspicious Bhāgīrathī;
King Nala of virtuous fame, Janārdana of virtuous fame, / Vaidehī of virtuous fame, and Yudhiṣṭhira of virtuous fame;
Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, and Vibhīṣaṇa, / Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma—these seven are long-lived ones.
The human who constantly remembers these upon rising at dawn / is freed from sins such as slaying a brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
When uttered once, dear one, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; / one enjoys the fruit of a gift of a hundred thousand cows.
And then, in a pure place, one should void feces and urine; / facing south at night, during the day one should face north.
Thereafter, a tooth-stick of grasses, udumbara, and the like; / and after this, the twice-born should be self-restrained at the twilight devotion.
In the morning red-colored, but at midday white-colored, / in the evening dark: the twice-born should meditate on Sarasvatī according to the rule.
Then, one should perform bathing with effort, according to knowledge. / Having washed the limbs, one should then smear them with clay:
on the region of the head, on the forehead, on the nose, on the heart, on the eyebrows, / on the two arms, on the flanks, likewise on the navel, on the two knees, and on both feet.
One [portion of] clay on the penis, three on the anus, ten on the left hand, / seven on both hands must be applied by one seeking purification.
'O earth traversed by a horse, traversed by a chariot, traversed by Viṣṇu, supporter of wealth! / O earth, take away the sin previously accumulated by me.'
Whoever casts clay on the body with this very mantra, / all his sins are destroyed, and the human becomes pure.
Then, the wise person should perform the bath preceded by Vedic [mantras] / in a male river, in a river, likewise in a well, in a pond, [or] in a pool,
in a body of water, or at an embankment; likewise, a mortal should properly perform / the superior jar-bath for the destruction of all sins.
Morning bathing brings great merit and destroys all sins; / the vipra who constantly performs it is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Near the morning twilight devotion, for as long as four daṇḍas, / for that long the water stands as nectar for the ancestors.
Beyond that, for a span of two ghaṭikās up to one yāma, for daily rites, / water during that time is equal to honey, increasing the satisfaction of the ancestors.
After that, for one and a half yāmas, the water is considered to consist of milk; / the water remains mixed with milk for four daṇḍas.
After this, the water [remains ordinary] drinkable water for three praharas; / beyond that, it is declared to be blood until the sun has set.
If one bathes in the fourth prahara or propitiates the ancestors at night, / that water is considered to belong to demons, except during an eclipse.
Drinkable water was created by me long ago for the accomplishment of all purposes; / and yakṣas are the bearers of the burden for the protection of that water.
Ancestors who have gone to another world do not obtain it; / water is difficult for them to obtain except from their own [kin] dwelling as mortals.
Therefore, libation must be offered by disciples, sons, grandsons, daughter's sons, and others, / and likewise by the circle of kin and others observing vows for the ancestors.
Nārada said: / Tell me the deity of water, and the rule of libation; / you ought to speak truly, O Lord of the gods, so that I may know.
Brahmā said: / Viṣṇu is proclaimed the deity of water in all the worlds; / he who becomes purified by water becomes Viṣṇu, he becomes Śaṅkara.
Having drunk merely a mouthful of water, a man becomes purified; / especially through contact with kuśa grass, water is superior to ambrosia.
Darbha grass, an abode of all the gods, was created by me in former times; / Brahmā resides at the root of kuśa, and Keśava in the middle of kuśa.
Know Śaṅkara to be at the tip of kuśa; these reside in kuśa. / With kuśa in hand, one is always pure if one recites a hymn or a mantra.
Everything is declared a hundredfold [more fruitful], and at a sacred ford it is said to be a thousandfold. / Kuśa, kāśa, and dūrvā, barley leaves, paddy,
balvaja, and puṇḍarīka are proclaimed as the seven varieties of kuśa. / In order, these established varieties of kuśa are pure in the world.
Whatever bath is without a mantra becomes completely fruitless; / and through contact with sesame, it becomes sweeter than nectar.
Therefore, the wise person should daily propitiate the ancestors with sesame and water; / with ten sesames, there is supreme satisfaction for the ancestors.
Out of fear of blocking the fire, the gods do not desire too much detail. / Whoever, having bathed, daily propitiates the ancestors with waters mixed with sesame,
by the release of a dark bull, by sesame water on the new moon, / [and] by the gift of a lamp in the rainy season, becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Whoever propitiates the ancestors with sesames on the new moon for one year / attains the status of a Vināyaka and is worshiped by all the gods.
And whoever propitiates the ancestors with sesames on all yugādi days— / that is declared to be a hundred times greater than [what is obtained] on the new moon.
On a solstice, on an equinox, on a full moon, and on a new moon, / having propitiated the host of ancestors, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Likewise on a manvantara day, on any other auspicious occasion, / during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, [and] at holy sacred fords such as Gayā.
Having gratified the ancestors, one goes to the abode of Mādhava; / therefore, having reached an auspicious day, one should gratify the assembly of ancestors.
Having first performed the offering of water to the deities with a concentrated mind, / the wise person then becomes eligible for the offering of water to the ancestors.
At a funeral rite and at the time of eating, one should cause [water] to be given with one hand; / at the water offering, one should give with both [hands]; this is the eternal rule.
Facing south, pure, one should gratify the ancestors / with the words, 'May they be satisfied,' followed again by name and clan.
If through delusion one should gratify the assembly of ancestors with non-black sesame seeds, / or if the giver, standing in water, offers water onto the ground,
that gift is given in vain; it does not reach anyone. / But if a man, standing on dry land, offers water into the water,
that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless. / But he who, wearing wet garments, performs the water offering in water—
his ancestors are satisfied, together with the gods, forever, O sinless one. / Wise poets know that a garment washed by washermen is impure;
Upon washing with the hand, the garment becomes pure again. / When one gratifies the ancestors in a pure spot, wearing dry garments,
the ancestors are certainly pleased tenfold thereby. / Bathing and twilight worship on a stone, a sword, or a copper vessel—
and whoever performs a water offering [there] obtains a hundredfold more for each. / When one gratifies the ancestors wearing a silver ring on the forefinger,
everything becomes a hundred-thousandfold; it is not otherwise. / Likewise, the wise man, wearing a gold ring on the ring finger,
should gratify the host of ancestors; it becomes a hundred-thousand-crore-fold. / Holding a sword-blade between the thumb and forefinger of the right hand,
or holding a gem with the ring finger, the water-hollow offering brings inexhaustible fruit. / As one goes for bathing, the gods together with the ancestor hosts,
having become wind, follow behind, afflicted with thirst and seeking water; / they turn away disappointed by the wringing out of one's garment.
Therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having performed the water offering to the ancestors. / As many as three and a half crores of bodily hairs exist on a human,
so many holy bathing places flow [there]; therefore, one should not wring it out. / The gods drink from the head, the ancestors from the beard,
the Gandharvas from the eyes, and all creatures from below. / The gods, all the hosts of ancestors, the Gandharvas, and creatures
are satisfied merely by the bath; no sin remains from bathing. / And the man who performs a daily bath is an excellent person;
Freed from all sins, he is honored in various worlds. / The gods and the great sages consider bathing to culminate in the water offering;
Beyond that, the wise man should cause worship of the gods to be performed. / Whoever worships Gaṇeśa has no obstacles arise for him.
And [one should worship] Sūrya for health, Mādhava for dharma and liberation, / Śiva for desire for rites, and Caṇḍikā for all desires.
Having worshipped the gods, one should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation; / then, having performed the fire-rite, the sacrifice, and the gratification of Brahmins,
of the deities and of all beings, one goes again to heaven. / Having made firm coming and going, desires, liberation, happiness, and heaven,

one should therefore perform the daily rites with every effort.
Nārada said: / For what reason, O father, do the gods together with the ancestor hosts

not obtain water, O omniscient one, in the way that mortals obtain it?
Brahmā said: / In the past, water, the nectar made of all deities, was created by me.
And for his protection, Rākṣasas and Yakṣas bear bows; / they slay an ancestor, a god, [or] from our words a man.
Animals, birds, and insects abiding in the mortal world, / and the gods who are born among mortals, and likewise surely human beings,
having daily offered water libations to the teacher, are established in the celestial realm. / One who does not bathe consumes filth, and one who does not recite prayers consumes pus and blood.
Without daily offering water libations, one becomes the killer of his ancestors; / and in not worshipping the gods, [there is] a sin equal to killing a brāhmaṇa.

And without performing the twilight rite, the evildoer slays the sun.
Nārada said:
Tell of the good conduct and sequence of rites for a brāhmaṇa,
from good conduct [one gains] heaven and liberation; good conduct destroys inauspicious signs. / For an ill-behaved man becomes censured in the world,
and constantly partakes of suffering, diseased, and short-lived indeed; / and by misconduct, a man’s dwelling in hell is assured.
And from good conduct [one attains] the higher world. Hear of conduct in accordance with reality: / One should daily smear the house with cow dung.
Then one should wash a wooden seat, a wooden vessel, and a stone slab. / A bronze vessel is purified with ash, but copper with acid;
a stone vessel with oil, a plowshare with horsehair [and cow dung], / but a vessel of gold, silver, or the like is purified with water alone;
an iron vessel with fire, and by cooking and washing. / Through digging, burning, smearing, and scrubbing,
and by the rain of Parjanya, impure earth is purified. / For metallic things, jewels, and whatever is made of stone,
purification with ashes and earth was declared by me in ancient times. / One’s bed, wife, child, clothing, sacred thread, and water-pot
are declared pure for oneself, never for others. / One should not eat in a single garment, nor bathe in a single garment;
one should never wear another's bathing cloth. / One should carry out the cleaning of hair and teeth early in the morning.
And one should daily offer obeisance to elders. / One should dine with the five wet: hands, feet, and mouth.
One who eats with five wet lives a hundred years. / One must not intentionally cross the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king,
or of a snātaka, an ācārya, an initiated person, or an educated brāhmaṇa. / A herd of cows, a deity, a brāhmaṇa, ghee, honey, a crossroads,
and renowned sacred trees one should circumambulate. / Between a cow and a brāhmaṇa, fire and a brāhmaṇa, two brāhmaṇas, or a married couple,
one should not walk between them; even one residing in heaven would surely fall. / Being impure from food, one should not touch fire, a brāhmaṇa, a deity, a teacher,
one's own head, a flowering tree, a sacrificial tree, or an unrighteous person. / One should never look at the three luminaries while impure from food:
the sun and moon, and the constellations everywhere. / [While impure from food] one should not look upon a brāhmaṇa, a teacher, a deity, a king, the best of ascetics,
a yogin, one performing divine rites, or a twice-born telling the laws. / On the banks of rivers, or at the ocean, lord of rivers,
at the base of a sacrificial tree, in a park, or in a flower garden, / nor in water should one discharge the bodily wastes,
nor in a brāhmaṇa’s residence, a cow-pen, or pleasant royal roads. / A wise man should never have shaving performed on the day of Mars [Tuesday].
One should not keep dirt on a tooth, nor put a nail in the mouth. / One should not perform an oil-massage on the days of the Sun [Sunday] and Mars [Tuesday].
One should not beat one’s limbs or seat, nor share a single seat with a teacher. / One must not seize the property of a learned brāhmaṇa, a deity, or a teacher,
nor of a king, ascetics, a lame person, a blind person, or a woman. / Way should be given to a brāhmaṇa, to cows, and to kings,
to a sick person, one burdened by a load, a pregnant woman, and a weak person. / One should not engage in dispute with kings, brāhmaṇas, or physicians.
One should avoid from afar a wicked brāhmaṇa and a teacher’s wife, / a fallen person, a leper, a Cāṇḍāla, and a cow-eater.
One should avoid from afar one who is cast out and devoid of knowledge; / and an evil, ill-behaved woman who bestows slander,
who acts wickedly, is vicious, ever fond of quarrelling, / wanton, having extra limbs, shameless, roaming outside,
spendthrift, and of bad conduct, one should avoid from afar. / One should never pay homage to a teacher's wife who is impure;
and an intelligent man must not touch her; having touched her, he is purified by bathing. / And one must always avoid playful dalliance with her;
one should certainly hear her words, but not gaze upon a teacher's wife, / nor a son's or brother's bride, or one's own young daughter.
And another teacher's wife one should not gaze upon, nor make contact with. / Conversation with them, as well as looking with knitted eyebrows,
quarrel, and shameless speech one should always avoid. / And one should never place one’s foot upon husks, charcoal, bones, or ashes,
cotton-seeds, religious remnants, funeral wood, a pyre, or a teacher. / One should not consume dry fish, foul-smelling food, or unclean matter,
food-remnants, other leftovers, or food cooked for another. / One should not stand or go, even for a moment, with wicked people;
a wise man should not stay for a moment in the shadow of a lamp or beneath a Kali tree. / Conversation with untouchables, the fallen, and the angry,
one should not do even for a moment; having done so, one would go to Raurava. / One should not pay homage to a younger brother, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle [as an elder],
yet having risen, one should give a seat, standing before them with joined palms. / To one smeared with oil, one impure from food, one wearing wet clothes, or a sick person,
one who has gone to the opposite shore, one distressed, or one carrying a burden, one should not offer salutation; / nor to one engaged in sacrifice, one ruined, one sporting with women,
one engaged in children's play, or one adorned with flowers and kuśa grass. / Covering the head or the ears, or with topknot untied in the water,
without having washed the feet, one should not sip water facing the south. / Devoid of the sacred thread, naked, with the tuck of the loincloth undone,
or covered by only a single cloth, having sipped water, one is not at all purified. / One should first touch the mouth with the three middle fingers;
and thereafter the nose with the thumb and forefinger; / and one should touch both eyes with the thumb and ring finger;
the two ears with the little finger and thumb, and the navel with the thumb; / having placed [the hand] on the heart with the palm, and upon the head with all fingers,
and touching both arms with the tips [of the fingers], then a man becomes purified. / Having performed water-sipping in this manner, a man becomes pure;
freed from all sins, he enjoys imperishable heaven. / Prāṇa is [satisfied] by the horn-gesture of three folds; and vyāna and apāna by the mudrā,
samāna by all [fingers], and udāna without the forefinger. / Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya:
these secondary breaths are pleased when [food] is offered to them on the ground. / Sleeping [should be done] with wet feet, and eating with dry feet;
and one should not sleep or eat in darkness. / And one should not perform cleaning of the teeth towards the west or south.
And one should never sleep with the head towards the north or the west; / from such sleep one's lifespan goes to destruction, and the man becomes a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, one should not sleep [facing north or west]; facing east or south is praised. / Facing east, one eats for long life; facing south, for dishonour;
Facing west, one eats for prosperity; facing north, one eats for fame. / Facing east, a man attains long life; facing south, he obtains the state of a ghost;
Facing west, he becomes diseased; and facing north, [he obtains] life and wealth. / The gods eat once [a day], but a man should eat twice;
A ghost or Daitya eats thrice, and a goblin eats a fourth time. / The gods consume meatless oblations; humans eat fish, meat, and the like;
Others eat putrid, stale, and corrupted food uncovered. / For those who dwell in heaven, four things dwell in their heart here in the world of living beings:
Praiseworthy charity, sweet speech, worship of the gods, and satisfying the brāhmaṇas. / A miserly disposition, blaming one's own kin, wearing rags, and devotion to base people,
Excessive anger, and bitter speech—these are the mark of a man who has come from hell. / Speech resembling fresh butter, a heart tender with compassion—
This is the visible characteristic of those born from the seed of dharma. / A heart devoid of compassion, speech harsh as a saw—
This is the visible characteristic of those born from the seed of sin. / If a man recites or listens to [these rules on] proper conduct and the rest,
Having obtained the fruit of proper conduct and the like, purified from sin, he is imperishable in heaven.

1.50.m: Bhīṣma said: / That merit which is supreme in the world, always agreed upon by all, / speak of that at your pleasure, O vipra, which was practiced by the ancient ancestors.
Pulastya said: / Once, all the twice-born disciples of Vyāsa together, out of respect, / bowed down to Vyāsa and asked him about dharma, just as you [now ask] me.
The twice-born said: / What is the holiest of the holy in the world, the best among all dharmas? / Tell us what human beings do to enjoy imperishable heaven.
Tell us of a single sacrifice attainable without hardship, pure, / suitable for the castes residing in the mortal world, both for the great and the lowly,
By doing which a man becomes worthy of worship among the gods in heaven. / Speak of all that to us, O brahman; be gracious in accordance with dharma.
Vyāsa said: / I will speak five narratives; listen to them first. / By performing just one of the five, one may attain liberation, heaven, and renown:
Worship of one's parents, and of one's husband; impartiality toward all beings; / harmlessness toward friends; and devotion to Viṣṇu: these are the five great sacrifices.
The dharma that a man accomplishes through worship of his parents first, O vipras, / is not attained even by hundreds of sacrifices, pilgrimages, and the like on earth.
The father is dharma, the father is heaven, the father is indeed the highest austerity; / when the father is pleased, all the deities are pleased.
He whose parents are satisfied by service and good qualities, / for him a bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day.
The mother embodies all sacred places; the father embodies all gods. / He who circumambulates his mother and father,
By him the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated. / He whose knees, hands, and head bow down to his parents
And fall upon the earth attains imperishable heaven. / As long as the dust marks from their feet remain clinging
To the limbs and head, so long is their son purified. / The son who drinks the water that washed the lotus feet of his parents,
His sins accumulated over hundreds of millions of births are destroyed. / Blessed is that man in the world, purified from all wickedness.
In a single birth a man attains leadership. / But the lowest of men who transgresses his parents in words
Must dwell in hell until the dissolution of all beings. / The lowest of sons who eats without having worshipped his parents
Remains in the hell of the pit of worms until the end of an eon. / Abandoning a father who is sick, old, impoverished in livelihood,
Or impaired in eyes and ears, one would go to the Raurava hell, / and is born among outcasts, Mlecchas, and Cāṇḍālas.
Neglecting the maintenance of one's parents causes the destruction of all merit. / A son who does not revere his parents, even though he frequents sacred places and gods,
Does not obtain their fruit; he wanders the earth like a worm. / I shall tell an ancient tale; O vipras, listen attentively,
Hearing which you will never again fall into delusion on earth. / Long ago, there was a twice-born known as Narottama.
Disregarding his own parents, he went to visit sacred places. / Then, as that brāhmaṇa traveled to all the sacred places,
His bathing clothes would dry in the sky day after day. / Pride entered the mind of that brāhmaṇa:
'There is none equal to me in meritorious deeds, illustrious in fame.' / When he spoke thus, a crane defecated on his face.
Incited by rage, the twice-born cursed the crane; / and the crane fell to the earth, its body reduced to ashes.
Fear and great confusion entered the chief of the twice-born at that fatal act; / then, because of that sin, the vipra's cloth would not go into the sky.
He immediately felt dejection; then the sky spoke to him: / 'Go, O brāhmaṇa, to the mute Cāṇḍāla, who is supremely righteous.
There you will learn dharma; his words will bring you welfare.' / Having heard that voice from the sky, he went to the house of Mūka.
He saw him serving his parents in all undertakings, / properly giving them warm water in the cold season,
Oil, heating, betel, and a cotton-filled blanket, / daily meals of sweet food, as well as milk and candied sugar,
Offering them sweet-scented floral garlands in spring, / and whatever other enjoyable things and various services [there were].
In the heat he also constantly fanned both parents. / Then, having attended to them, he always took his food.
He would relieve their fatigue and likewise their distress. / Through these merits Viṣṇu stayed within his house for a long time.
Sporting in the mid-air without supporting pillars, / the Lord of the three worlds was constantly present in his mansion,
Assuming the lovely form of a vipra, unsurpassed, not seen as such by others, / full of splendour, of great being, beautifying the dwelling.
Filled with amazement at seeing him, the vipra said to Mūka: / The vipra said: 'Come near me; I wish to learn from you the eternal
Good of myself and of all the worlds; you ought to tell it truly.' / Mūka said: 'I am worshipping my parents today; how can I come to your side?
Only after worshipping my parents will I do your business. / Stand by the doorway; I will offer you hospitality.'
When this was said by the cāṇḍāla, the brāhmaṇa then grew angry: / 'Having abandoned me, a brāhmaṇa, what greater duty do you have?'
Mūka said: / 'Why do you get angry in vain, O vipra? I am not your crane now. / Your anger succeeded with the crane, not anywhere else.
Your bathing cloth does not dry or remain in the sky; / having heard the voice from the sky, you came to my house.
Wait, wait, and I will speak; if not, go to the devoted wife; / and having seen her, O best of the twice-born, your cherished desire will bear fruit.'
Then the all-pervading Viṣṇu, bearing the form of a twice-born, came out of his house / and said to the twice-born: "I am going to her house."
Having reflected, that best of the twice-born walked along with him; / as he was going, the twice-born, filled with wonder, said this to Hari:
"Why is it, twice-born, that you continually reside inside the house of an outcaste, / surrounded by women, father, with joy?"
Hari said: / "Truly, your mind has not become pure even now; / after seeing the devoted wife and the rest, you will surely know me later."
The twice-born said: / "And who is that devoted wife, father? Or what great fame does she possess, / because of which I should go there? Tell me the reason, twice-born."
Hari said: / "Among rivers, the Jāhnavī is best; among women, the devoted wife; / among mortals, the protector of the people; and among gods, Janārdana.
A woman who is a devoted wife, constantly intent on her husband's welfare, / delivers a hundred men each of both lineages.
She enjoys heaven for as long as the dissolution of creatures lasts; / fallen from heaven, her husband becomes a sovereign king.
Becoming his chief queen, she subsequently finds happiness; / time and again heaven and royal power are theirs without doubt.
Having thus attained a hundred births, in the end liberation surely occurs." / The twice-born said: "Who is a devoted wife? What are her characteristics?
Tell me, tiger among the twice-born, so that I may know in truth." / Hari said: "A woman who loves her husband a hundredfold more than her son, and serves him as a king out of awe,
and sees her husband as Śauri—she is a devoted wife; / a maidservant in tasks, a courtesan in lovemaking, like a mother in offering food,
a wise counselor to her husband in times of distress—she is a devoted wife; / she who does not transgress her husband's command with mind, speech, or physical action,
who always eats after her husband has eaten—she is a devoted wife; / on whatever bed her husband sleeps with care,
there she continually worships her husband; / she never harbors envy, nor miserliness, nor is she arrogant;
she who looks upon honor and dishonor as equal—she is a devoted wife; / she who, seeing an attractive man, regards him as a brother, father, or son,
and as another [she is] a virtuous woman—she is a devoted wife; / go to her, tiger among the twice-born, and speak according to your desire.
Eight wives of his live there, and among them is a fair-complexioned woman, / endowed with beauty and youth, full of compassion, renowned,
known by the name Śubhā; having gone to her, ask about your welfare." / Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Seeing his disappearance, the twice-born was then astonished; / and he, having gone to the house of the virtuous woman, questioned the devoted wife.
Hearing the guest's voice, the virtuous woman came out of the house in haste; / seeing the twice-born there, she stood at the doorway.
And seeing her, the best of the twice-born joyfully spoke these words: / "Tell me what is dear and beneficial to me, just as you have seen it."
The devoted wife said: "Right now I am serving my husband, and I have no independence; / afterwards I will attend to your matter; receive hospitality today."
The twice-born said: "In my body there is no hunger, nor thirst, nor exhaustion today; / speak my desired wish, auspicious one, or else I will place a curse upon you."
Then she said to him: "I am not the crane, best of the twice-born; / go to the righteous Tulādhāra and ask him about your welfare, twice-born."
Having spoken thus, that fortunate woman went inside the house; / there the twice-born saw a brāhmaṇa, as in the dwelling of a cāṇḍāla.
Having reflected, filled with astonishment, the twice-born went along with him; / and he saw that twice-born standing there with a glad heart.
Joyfully seeing that twice-born and that virtuous woman, he spoke: / "What happened in another land was indeed told by her!
How does the outcaste know my conduct, and how does the devoted wife? / Therefore I wonder, father; what is this supremely great marvel?"
Hari said: "The reason for everything is known, father, by the well-wishers of all beings, / because of supreme merit and virtuous conduct, which has made you astonished.
And what did she say to you? Speak that now, sage." / The twice-born said: "She directed me to ask the righteous Tulādhāra."
Hari said: "Come, tiger among sages, I will go to him." / And as Hari was walking, he asked: "Where is Tulādhāra situated?"
Hari said: "Where there is a crowd of people in the fair sale of many goods, / selling and buying here and there, is Tulādhāra.
Barley, essence, oil, and a heap of grain—people take everything / and give it right from his presence.
Even when the end of his life was at hand, abandoning truth, / a lie was never spoken by that best of excellent men; therefore he holds the scale of righteousness."
When this was said, he saw him selling many liquids, / a mortal bearing filthy mud, smeared with slime on the buds of his teeth.
speaking various words there concerning goods and wealth, / surrounded on all sides by mortals of many kinds, by women and men.
He addressed him with sweet speech, saying, "How, how? / Explain righteousness to me; I have come near you for my benefit."
Tulādhāra said: "As long as people remain in my very presence, twice-born, / so long I have no leisure, until the night watch.
Taking that instruction, go to Dharmākara; / concerning the fault in the death of the crane and the non-drying of the cloth in the sky,
you will know all of that there; go to Sajjanādrohaka; / there, through his instruction, your desire will bear fruit."
Having said this, Tulādhāra carries out buying and selling. / 'Likewise, dear father, I will go to him who harms good people.'
from Tulādhāra's direction, I do not know his dwelling." / Hari said: "Come, let us go; I will go together with you to his house."
Then, as they went along the path, the brāhmaṇa spoke to Hari; / the twice-born said: "For Tulādhāra there is neither bathing nor libation to gods and ancestors,
his limbs are smeared with dirt, and all his clothing is tainted; / how does he know what happened to me in another country?
Therefore I wonder, father; tell me the whole reason." / Hari said: "By truth and an equanimous mind, the three worlds have been conquered by him.
Through that, the ancestors and the gods together with the hosts of sages are pleased; / and through that, the righteous man knows what happened in the past and the future.
There is no higher duty than truth; there is no greater sin than falsehood, / especially for a man who is sinless and of an equanimous mind.
He whose mind becomes equal towards an enemy, a friend, or an indifferent person, / has all sins destroyed and attains union with Viṣṇu.
One who always conducts himself in this way delivers ten million kinsmen: / truth, self-restraint, tranquility, courage, steadfastness, absence of greed,
absence of astonishment, freedom from sloth—all these are established in him; / by that, the knower of duty knows entirely what happens
in the world of the gods and the world of mortals; Hari resides in his body; / there is no one equal to him in the world, equal in truth and uprightness,
and he is righteousness personified; by him alone the world is sustained." / The twice-born said: "Through your grace I have understood the cause regarding Tulādhāra."
"Tell what the conduct of Adrohaka was, if you please." / Hari said: "Formerly, a prince had a high-born wife in the prime of her youth,
like Kāmadeva's wife [Rati], or Vāsava's [Śacī]; / his wife was as dear to him as life, a beautiful woman named Sundarī.
Suddenly he had to set out on the king's business; / he pondered in his mind about her who was dearer than life itself:
'In what place can I leave her so that she will definitely be protected?' / Having considered this, he went in haste to that man's house.
And he spoke those words to him. Hearing them, he was amazed: / 'I am neither your father, nor your brother, nor your relative;
I am not a friend of her father's or mother's family. / How then, my friend, could you feel at ease with her staying in my house?'
Meanwhile, he replied with appropriate words: / 'In the world there is no one like you, who knows dharma and has subdued his senses.'
He [the host] said to him: 'Even knowing all, you should not speak faultily. / What man is capable of guarding a wife who enchants the three worlds?'
The prince said: 'Having examined [all men] on the earth, I came to you. / Let her remain in your house; I am going to my own residence.'
When this was said, he spoke again: 'In this splendid city / full of many lustful men, how can a woman be protected?'
And he said to him again: 'Protect her, and I shall depart.' / Out of a dilemma of duty, the householder said to the prince:
'I will do an improper act; serving you is proper and beneficial. / But such a wife must always stay in my house, my friend,
under god-like guardianship. Say if you desire this pleasing arrangement: / she must lie on my bed along with me and my wife.
If you regard your own [sense of] deity [as satisfied], let her stay; if not, let her go.' / Reflecting for a moment, the prince then said to him:
'So be it, my friend; do as you please.' / Then he spoke to his wife: 'Whatever is auspicious or inauspicious according to his word,
must be done; you bear no fault, by my command, O beautiful one.' / Having said this, he departed by the command of his father, the king.
Thereafter, at night, it was done just as said: / the righteous man always slept between the two women.
Even so, he did not stray from dharma. Between his own wife and the wife of another, / from touching his own wife, his mind felt desire;
but from contact with that [other woman], he regarded her as a daughter. / When her breasts repeatedly touched his back,
he thought of them as the breasts of a mother to a small boy, her son; / and when her limbs repeatedly touched his limbs,
he considered her day by day as a son [considers] his mother. / From then on, all intimate contact with his own wife ceased.
Thus, after half a year, her husband returned to the city / and inquired among the people about her conduct as reported.
Some informed him of good, though they, as young men, were quite astonished; / others said: 'Given by you, she sleeps with him.
From the joint contact of a man and a woman, how could there be composure? / Even if not asked, a young man would say that he desires her.'
By the power of his merit, he heard this ill report of the people; / to free himself from public slander, an auspicious thought occurred to him.
Gathering wood himself, he kindled a great fire. / At that moment, my friend, the glorious prince
came immediately to his house and saw him and the woman— / the woman with a beaming face, and the man sunk in despair.
Discerning their state of mind, the prince spoke these words: / 'Why do you not converse with me, a friend who has returned after a long time?'
He too, righteous and undamaged in mind, said to the prince: / 'The difficult deed that I performed for your sake,
I consider completely wasted because of the gossip of the people. / Today I will enter the fire; let men and gods watch.'
Having spoken thus, that illustrious one entered the fire; / as he entered the fire, there was not a flower [scorched] in the dwelling of his hair.
nor his limb was burned by the fire, nor his garment, nor a lock of hair. / In the sky all the gods joyfully cried: 'Well done! Well done!'
Showers of flowers fell upon his head from all around. / And on all those who had spoken evil words against those two,
various kinds of leprosy broke out upon their mouths. / Arriving there, the gods joyfully pulled him out of the fire.
Astonished sages worshipped him with lovely flowers. / When that very radiant man was thus honored by all the foremost sages
and by various people, he worshipped them all. / The name Sajjanādrohaka ('he who harms no good man') was bestowed on him by gods, asuras, and humans.
Purified by the dust of his feet, the earth became filled with crops. / And the gods said to the prince there: 'Receive your wife back.
An equal to him has never existed, nor will ever exist in the world; / at present there is no man on earth not conquered by lust and greed.
For gods, asuras, humans, rakṣasas, beasts, and birds, / and all creatures beginning with insects, this lust is very difficult to overcome.
It is born continually in living beings from lust, greed, and anger; / lust binds the cycle of existence; absence of desire is nowhere to be found.
By him alone have all the fourteen worlds been conquered. / In his heart Vāsudeva constantly abides with joy.
Thus by touching and seeing him, human beings are purified of all stain / and, becoming sinless, attain imperishable heaven.'
Having spoken thus, the gods joyfully departed to heaven in their celestial chariots; / the humans went their way contented, and the husband and wife went to their house.
Then divine vision was granted to him: he could see the gods, / and he easily understood the news of the three worlds fully.
Then along his path, he was seen together with him. / He asked him with joy: 'Speak on the instruction of dharma that is beneficial.'
Sajjanādroha said: 'Go, O brāhmaṇa who knows dharma, to the Vaiṣṇava Puruṣottama; / having seen him, what you desire will now bear fruit.
You know whether it is the death of the crane or the drying of the cloth, / and what other desire is situated in your heart.'
Hearing these words, he went towards the Vaiṣṇava; / he went joyfully together with that brāhmaṇa of the form of Viṣṇu.
He saw a pure man standing before him, blazing, / endowed with all auspicious marks, radiant with his own splendor.
That righteous man, recounting whatever had happened, / said to the beloved of Hari seated in meditation: 'I have come to you from afar.'
The Vaiṣṇava said: 'The best of gods, the enemy of the Dānavas, is always pleased with you. / Seeing you, our mind is filled with joy now, O brāhmaṇa.
Unrivalled welfare is yours today; your wish will bear fruit. / Your cloth constantly dries in the sky; it cannot be otherwise,
since you have seen the God, the best of the deities, Hari, abiding in my house.' / When the Vaiṣṇava had said this, he then spoke to him again:
'Where does that Viṣṇu always abide? Show Him today by your grace.' / The Vaiṣṇava said: 'Having entered into this delightful temple, the Supreme Lord—'

"Seeing him, you will be freed from terrible sin and from the bonds of rebirth."
Having heard his words, [the brāhmaṇa] entered the dwelling,

and saw Viṣṇu, that twice-born one, resting upon a lotus-bed.
Bowing with his head, he then joyfully seized his feet:

"Be gracious, O Lord of gods! I did not know you before.
Here and in the next world, O Lord of gods, I am your servant, O master.

Your grace has been seen by me, O Madhusūdana.
I wish to see your form, if there is mercy toward me."

Viṣṇu said:
"O earthly deity, I indeed always have affection for you.
Out of love, I have brought about the vision of virtuous people [for you].

By seeing, touching, meditating upon, praising, and conversing [with them],
even once, only the virtuous attain imperishable heaven.

Indeed, through constant association [with them], there is destruction of all sins;
and having enjoyed endless happiness, one dissolves into my body.

Having bathed at holy pilgrimage sites, and having seen me everywhere,
and having seen the lands of the virtuous, one dissolves into my body.

Having always recounted sacred stories in front of people,
that tiger among men dissolves into my body.

Fasting on my day, hearing my deeds with devotion,
and keeping a vigil through the night, one dissolves into my body.

Ever loudly proclaiming [my praise], with dance, song, instrumental music, and the like,
remembering the name, O best of the twice-born, one dissolves into my body.

You are my devotee and a sacred pilgrimage site. For the release from the sin
that arose from killing the crane, standing, O friend, he said:

'Go to the great-souled Mūka, a sacred pilgrimage site, the best among the virtuous.
By seeing Mūka, my dear, all great people have been seen.'

Only from seeing them, and likewise from conversing [with them], and from connection
with me, you have come to my home.

He whose sins have been destroyed through thousands of millions of births,
he, O knower of dharma, sees me, just as by that [devotion] grace is achieved.

It is only through my grace, O child, that I have been seen by you, O sinless one.
Therefore, choose a boon whatever is in your mind."

Mādhava said:
"Since such an understanding always shines in you, O sinless one,
therefore you shall attain enjoyments like mine in my abode.

However, your parents have not received worship from you, O sinless one.
Only after honoring your parents will you later attain my body.

By the breath of their sighs and by their anger, repeatedly and intensely,
your ascetic heat trickles away constantly; therefore, worship them, O twice-born one!

Upon whichever son the anger of his parents continually falls,
from that hell neither I, nor the Creator, nor Śaṅkara can save him.

Therefore, go to your parents; perform their worship with diligence.
Then, through the grace of those two alone, proceed to my abode."
When this was said, the best of the twice-born spoke again to the teacher of the universe: / 'If you are pleased with me, O Lord, show me your own form, O Acyuta.'

Then, out of love for the twice-born, pleased in heart and self-controlled,
friendly to brāhmaṇas, he showed his own form to the one dedicated to sacred rites:

Puruṣottama, holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
the cause of the entire universe, filling the universe with splendor.

Bowing like a stick, the brāhmaṇa spoke again to Acyuta:
"Today my birth has borne fruit; today my two eyes are auspicious.

Today my two hands are praiseworthy; blessed am I, O Lord of the Universe!
Today my ancestors go to the eternal world of Brahmā.

My kinsmen rejoice today through your grace, O Janārdana;
and now all my desires are fulfilled.

Yet I have great astonishment, O Lord: how do those wise ones, Mūka and the others,
know my history, which took place in another land?

In the interior space of his house stood an exceedingly radiant brāhmaṇa;
likewise in the house of the faithful wife, and on the head of Tulādhāra,

and likewise in the home of the harmless one, and you in the abode of the Vaiṣṇava.
Out of grace to me, O brāhmaṇa, you ought to tell me truly."

Adroha has conquered greed and lust, and is remembered as a Vaiṣṇava devoted to me.
Pleased with their virtues, I happily abide in their dwellings,

together with Bhāratī and Kamalā, O best among the twice-born."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"Men become extreme sinners from association with a great sinner:
Thus the knowers of dharma always speak in the treatises of traditional law, / in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Vedas; how do you stay in a house?'

The Blessed Lord said:
"Mūka is the doer of all good things in the three worlds.
Even if an outcaste is established in proper conduct, the gods know him to be a brāhmaṇa.

There is no one equal to Mūka in the worlds in terms of virtuous deeds.
Ever devoted to service of his parents, by him the three worlds have been conquered.

Pleased by devotion to the two of them, I, along with all the hosts of gods,
abide in the form of a brāhmaṇa in the space inside his house;

likewise in the house of the faithful wife, in the dwelling of Tulādhāra,
in the house of Adroha, and in the home of the Vaiṣṇava.

I always abide there, O knower of dharma; I do not leave for an instant.
Therefore, even other people who commit sins see me constantly.

And because of virtue, I was seen by you on account of my grace.
Devoted to serving his parents, pure, the outcaste has attained godhood.

Therefore, I dwell in his house with joy together with him;
again and again I converse [with him], O delight of the twice-born.

Unimpeded in thought, I always abide in his mind;
he knows your history, and so do the faithful wife and the others.

I will tell their deeds; listen in regular order,
hearing which a mortal is completely freed from the bonds of rebirth.

There is no holy pilgrimage site superior to a father and a mother among the gods of gods.
He by whom the worship of his parents is performed is himself the supreme man.

The command of parents is equal in fruit to the command of a god and the command of a guru.
From their worship [one attains] the kingdom of heaven; by harming them, one goes to Raurava.

He is in my heart, and I abide in his heart;
there is no difference between us; in the next world and in this one he is equal to me.

In my presence, in my delightful city, together with all his kinsmen,
he will enjoy inexhaustible pleasure, and in the end he will dissolve into me.

Therefore, indeed, that Mūka knows the news occurring throughout the three worlds,
O tiger among men! Whence is this astonishment of yours?"

The twice-born one said:
"Not having performed the worship of parents out of delusion or ignorance,
or having known [it], what good or bad is to be done, O Lord of the Universe?"

The Blessed Lord said:
"He by whom devotion to parents has been performed for a single day, a month, two fortnights,
half a fortnight, or a year, he shall go to my abode.

Having caused pain to their mind, one inevitably goes to hell.
Whether the worship of parents was performed or not performed formerly,

a man, having performed the release of a bull, obtains the fruit of devotion to parents:
food, clothing, cow-products, food with meat or without meat.

All that is given to kinsmen is said to be multiplied a hundred thousand times
by that wise son by whom an ancestral rite has been performed with all his possessions."
He attains recollection of previous births and reaps the fruit of devotion to the ancestors; / in the three worlds, indeed, there is no greater sacrifice than a śrāddha.
Whatever little is given here, one enjoys all of it imperishably; / know that [given] to another it is ten-thousandfold, and to kinsmen it is said to be a hundred-thousandfold.
In the case of a funeral ball of rice, it is said to be ten-millionfold; given to a twice-born, it is said to be endless; / so too in the water of the Gaṅgā, at Gayā, at Prayāga, and at Puṣkara,
in Vārāṇasī, at the Siddhakuṇḍa, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. / Whoever offers an oblation of food [there]—liberation certainly belongs to him,
and the ancestors attain imperishable heaven, the fruit of his birth. / Especially on the Bhāgīrathī, whoever offers water with sesame seeds
attains the path of liberation; what then to say of the offering of funeral balls? / On riverbanks it is a-thousandfold, but on a great river it is held to be ten-thousandfold.
From combination with an ordinary fruit, the śrāddha becomes a-hundredfold. / On a new-moon day, on a yugādi day, and during an eclipse of the sun or moon,
whoever performs a pārvaṇa rite attains an imperishable realm. / All his ancestors are pleased for ten thousand years,
bestowing dear blessings and endless enjoyment upon the son. / Therefore, on a conjunction day, the pārvaṇa rite must be joyfully performed by sons.
Having performed this sacrifice for the two parents, one is released from the bondage of birth. / The śrāddha [performed] day after day is commemorated as the daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha).
Whoever causes it to be performed with faith attains an imperishable realm; / and likewise in the dark fortnight, a śrāddha for specific desires according to rule.
Having performed it, he attains the desired object, or whatever is in his heart. / Taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the limit, the fortnight that is the fifth—
one should perform the śrāddha there, whether [the sun] has entered Virgo or not. / When the sun has entered Virgo, the sixteen days that follow
are equal to Vedic sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial gifts. / This highly meritorious śrāddha for specific desires has arrived for him as auspicious.
If unable, one should perform it at the beginning of the dark fortnight when [the sun is] in Libra; / when the new-moon day enters Scorpio, the ancestors depart into despair.
They return to their own abode after uttering a very harsh curse; / by the curse of the ancestors, everything of the son is considered ruined.
Wealth, sons, fame, desired things, and life itself— / all these are obtained by human beings birth after birth
solely through the boon of the ancestors; therefore one should never abandon this. / Having performed the nāndīmukha rite at a marriage, a vow, a sacrifice, or the like, a twice-born
attains imperishable merit, and his lineage flourishes. / A man in whose case the opposite occurs goes to hell;
the destruction of his family occurs, and he lives a life of sorrow. / Then one should first worship Gaṇeśa, the son of Śambhu,
next the sixteen mothers, and after that the multitude of ancestors, / beginning with the paternal great-grandfather, among all the nāndīmukha ancestors.
In a nāndīmukha rite, the wise man should seat all the twice-born facing east; / he should pronounce the word "namaḥ" and elsewhere employ "svadhā".
Offering oblation-water and balls of rice during an eclipse of the moon or sun, / a man attains imperishable heaven and the increase of his ancestors' nourishment.
A man who does not bathe then, nor gives oblation-water and balls of rice / to the ancestors according to his capacity, goes to the state of a caṇḍāla.
Every gift is equal to [a gift of] land, all twice-born are equal to Vyāsa, / and all water is equal to the Gaṅgā when the moon is seized by Rāhu.
It is declared a-hundred-thousandfold during the moon, but a-millionfold during the sun; / when one has reached Gaṅgā water, it is ten million for the moon and a hundred million for the sun.
Whatever fruit comes from a hundred thousand cows properly given— / that same fruit is obtained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the moon is seized by Rāhu.
And during an eclipse of the moon or sun, whoever plunges into the Jāhnavī / has bathed in all holy places; why should he wander the earth?
A solar eclipse on a Sunday, and likewise a lunar eclipse on a Monday, / is renowned as "Cūḍāmaṇi" (the Crest-Jewel); endless fruit is commemorated on that occasion.
The man who, having fasted on both of those [occasions] before, gives a funeral ball, water, and gifts at a holy sacred site, is established in the world of Satya.

The twice-born said:
Such a great sacrifice and śrāddha for the father has been declared by you; / O dear one, what should indeed be done by a son in the final time and afterwards?
And having done what is the highest good easily attained birth after birth / by an intelligent son? O Lord, you should kindly tell [me].

The blessed Lord said:
