When early age is reached, the father is remembered as 'son', / and in the latter [age], the son is 'father', because of protecting, not indeed because of worshiping.
He should worship his father like a god, and show affection like to a son; / he should never transgress his command, even in his mind.
The son who remedies [the illness] of an afflicted father / attains imperishable heaven and is always worshiped by the gods.
Seeing the signs of death even of a father who is about to die, / the son, having performed a sacrifice, would attain equality with the gods.
Listen, I shall speak of the virtue of that wise son / who, by proper fasting alone, gives heaven to his father.
The merit of thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices / would accrue in [such] fasting; in a sacred site, it is multiplied ten million times over those two.
The supreme man who dies in the water of the Bhāgīrathī / will not drink the milk of a mother's breast; he reaches liberation.
He who voluntarily abandons his life-breaths in Vārāṇasī, / having enjoyed his desired fruit, dissolves into my body.
The state that belongs to sages joined with yoga, whose semen is drawn upward, / that state belongs to one who abandons life-breaths in the seven Brahmaputras.
Especially one who resorts to the northern bank of the Lohita / and abandons his life-breaths according to rule, attains equality with me.
And at the Urvaśīkeśa holy sacred site of that very [river], O best of twice-borns, / dead [there, he] is reborn, attains everything, and is not tainted by faults.
For him whose abandonment of life-breaths occurs inside a house, / for as long as a knot remains in the house, so long is there bondage for the body.
Year after year, one [knot] after another diminishes; / while his sons and kinsmen look on, there is no deliverance from bondage.
One who dies on a mountain, in a forest, in an inaccessible place, or in a waterless location, / meets an evil destiny and is born again as an insect and the like.
He whose funeral rite takes place on the following day after death / remains in the Kumbhīpāka [hell] for sixty thousand years.
If one dies impure from touching an untouchable, or as an outcaste, / he stays in hell for a very long time and is born among Mleccha castes.
Likewise, he is born among many insects and animal species; / therefore, after a long time, one should understand merit and demerit.
By merit and by the practice of merit of all who dwell in the mortal world, / whatever state occurs at the time of death for men, such a destiny comes to be.
He who dies at a holy sacred site while meditating on the names of Viṣṇu / is cleansed of sin, goes to heaven, and is not tainted by any faults.
The strong son who carries the body of his dead father / undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
First, the son should apply fire to the mouth on the father's body on the pyre / according to rule, purified by mantras; then he should burn the body.
'Endowed with greed and delusion, enveloped in sin and merit— / may I burn all his limbs; may he go to divine worlds!'
Having burned [it], the son should then pass over to the collection of the bones; / when the tenth day arrives, he should abandon his wet garment.
Cutting the red cloth, he should cast it into fire or water; / and then on the eleventh day, the wise man should perform the śrāddha.
He should feed one brāhmaṇa for the nourishment of the dead person's body; / and he should properly give a gift of clothing, a seat, and sandals.
Along with all utensils, equal to land, elephants, horses, and the like, / he should give a black cow for freedom from all sins.
On the fourth day, in the third fortnight, at six months, and at the year's end, / and the twelve monthly ones—these are the sixteen śrāddhas.
For him for whom these are not performed here according to capacity and with faith, / his ghostly state is permanent, even by hundreds of offered śrāddhas.
For a year he should give a water-pot and food combined with meat, / and daily; out of non-existence, one should satisfy [them] by fasting for a month.
When the year has passed, the wise one, best of twice-borns, / should have the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa śrāddha performed according to the rule of the Pārvaṇa.
Impurity for a father is for a year, and for a mother it is six months; / for a wife, three months; and half of that for a brother and son.
Impurity belongs to sapiṇḍas as long as he stays in the house; / listen, O dear one, I shall state what is forbidden for the son:
Chaste and well-conducted, he should never go to a woman; / after seven ghaṭīs and before nine ghaṭīs,
that time is known as kutapa; what is given to the ancestors [then] is imperishable. / Three are purifying in a śrāddha: a daughter's son, kutapa, and sesame seeds.
And three they praise here: truth, freedom from anger, and freedom from haste; / evening twilight worship, food of another, eating again, intercourse,
giving, and receiving a gift—having performed a śrāddha, he should avoid [these]. / Having done a hundred improper deeds, the wise man should perform a śrāddha;
and it attains the status of an obligation, as declared by Viriñci himself. / Listen, O son, I shall tell an ancient tale of many [men]:
Having killed the cow of their guru, they offered a śrāddha and went to heaven; / and by merely recounting them, a śrāddha becomes imperishable.
The seven disciples of the sage Vasiṣṭha, brāhmaṇas of virtuous vows— / when the ancestral śrāddha arrived, the beloved sacrificial cow of their guru
was requested and taken home with joy by the seven brothers; / having deliberated and killed that cow for beef in the ancestral sacrifice,
they gave meat to a priest and fed the remaining vipras. / Having completed the ancestral rites, taking the calf, those twice-born
delivered [it] to their guru, [saying,] 'The cow has been eaten by a tiger.' / Then, knowing their action purely through the power of his asceticism,
he cursed those disciples then: 'You will become Cāṇḍālas!' / Trembling then, those vipras stood with folded hands:
'Givers of cow's flesh in the ancestral rite always, O sinless one, / doing thousands of improper deeds and great sins,
acting in matters of the ancestors, they went to heaven, purified from sin! / Much ancient [lore] of various kinds has been heard from your mouth, O master;
you ought to pardon us, O knower of dharma! Let an end to the curse be ordained!' / Vasiṣṭha said: 'Your curse is according to your sin, not from a deliberation of dharma.
Born as Cāṇḍālas and the like, you will remember what happened previously; / and there will be no loss of knowledge for you, nor destruction of the Smṛti text.
Having crossed over the sinful birth, afterwards you will go to liberation.' / Then, having cast off their life-breaths due to the guru's curse, those twice-born
were born in a Cāṇḍāla womb, all endowed with knowledge; / breast milk was not drunk by them, remembering that previous birth.
Having died, they all were born as deer, and again in the forest as cakravāka birds; / then, O twice-born, they were born as white geese at the sacred site of Mānasa.
About to die, those fortunate ones died out of sorrow; / at that time there was a great king remembered as Dharmaketu.

Then, accompanied by his wife and retinue, he went to the holy place to bathe. / Then, through delusion, the three swans, thinking of kingdom, enjoyment, women,

and foods, departed at that time to another world: / "Having known the Veda and the Vedāṅga, we will attain liberation!"
Thinking thus, the others went from there to another world. / Then three became kings, and four became excellent brahmins.
Then in Kurukṣetra, by the power of their asceticism, they completely knew the Vedas / and Vedāṅgas, and the affairs of the next world and this world.
The three born into royal families were kings deluded by pride; / due to loss of knowledge, they did not know the higher world or their ultimate welfare.
And those brahmins, out of compassion, summoned their own servant: / "Go to the kings out of kindness and deliver this letter in haste:
'[Once] seven hunters in Daśārṇa, deer on Mount Kālañjara, / cakravāka birds in Śaradvīpa, swans in the Mānasa lake—
they have now been born in Kurukṣetra as brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. / They have set forth on the distant path; why do you despond?'"
Taking the letter, the servant showed it to the kings. / Seeing the letter, the kings abandoned their kingdom and went to the twice-born.
Having heard their words, those ascetics departed, / and in no long time they attained liberation together with them.
O twice-born, whoever hears this [story] beginning with the seven hunters at a śrāddha, / imperishable food and drink attend his ancestors.
The twice-born said: / How can the ancestral rite of an indigent brahmin be performed, / or that of an ascetic, a forest-dweller, or a householder, O Keśava?
The Blessed One said: / Having gathered grass and wood, or having begged for a cowrie-shell, / if he performs the rites for the ancestors, the fruit becomes a-hundred-thousandfold.
Whoever, having done a hundred forbidden deeds, performs the ancestral śrāddha— / destruction of all his sins occurs, and that man goes to heaven.
In the absence of everything, whoever gives grass to cows on the ancestor-tithi, / that man obtains a greater fruit than the offering of funeral balls.
Formerly, in the Vairāṭa region, an extremely wretched man wept; / when the ancestor-tithi arrived, he wept due to the lack of everything.
Having wept for a long time, he too asked a wise twice-born: / "O brahmin, on the ancestor-tithi today, what could be done that would be beneficial?
I do not have even a single cowrie-shell or wealth, O best of the knowers of Brahman! / Give me instruction so that I may abide in dharma."
The twice-born said: / "Go quickly to the forest, dear one, right now at the kutapa hour; / swiftly give grass to a cow, intending it for your father."
Then, by his instruction, having gathered a bundle of grass, / he gave it to a cow, delighted, for the nourishment of his father.
By the grace of this merit, he went to the abode of the gods; / and having enjoyed heaven for a very long time, he was born into a wealthy family.
Being wealthy because of his past merit from the sacrifice to the ancestors, / he offered the funeral ball to his father with all his possessions and wealth.
Then, from the spiritual practice of that single birth, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu; / having enjoyed endless happiness there, he became a sovereign universal monarch.
Since there is no duty whatever higher than the ancestral sacrifice, / therefore, with all effort and according to one's capacity, one should perform it without envy.
The man who recites this lineage of dharma in the presence of people / attains the fruit of bathing in the water of the Viṣṇupadī in every realm.
The heap of great sins that has been committed by him through birth after birth— / all that goes to destruction once this is uttered and heard.

1.51.m: Narottama said: / "He is the lord of the universe, of the thirty [gods] and of all other deities; / he is the master, the creator, the destroyer, the protector, the sustainer, the father, and the mother.
The weariness of our speech is relieved only by discoursing upon Viṣṇu. / Yet curiosity has arisen within me, like thirst or hunger.
When one asks about what has happened, it must indeed be told by a beloved one. / How does a devoted wife (pativratā) know even what is past, O Lord?
Or what power is within her? You ought to explain this in full." / The Blessed One said: / "I told you before, my child; yet curiosity arises again in you, O twice-born!
I will narrate all of that which dwells in your mind. / A devoted wife holds her husband as her life-breath and is always devoted to her husband's welfare.

She is to be worshipped even by the gods, and by sages who proclaim the Absolute (brahmavādin). / A woman who is devoted to a single husband is traditionally regarded as the most venerable in the world.
In honouring her, no burden will remain concealed. / Formerly, my dear child, in the central region (Madhyadeśa), there was a very beautiful city.
In that [city] lived a devoted wife of the brahmin caste named Sevyā. / Her husband had become a leper due to the impediment of his past karma.
Though his sores were suppurating, she was continually dedicated to his service. / Whatever desire he had, she fulfilled it with all her might.
She worshipped him daily like a god and showed him affection without malice. / One day, seeing an exceedingly beautiful courtesan walking along the road,
he was overcome by infatuation and his mind was seized by passion. / He let out a very long sigh and then became dejected.
Hearing him, the virtuous woman came out of the house and asked her husband: / 'Why are you dejected, my lord? Why this deep sigh, O master?
Tell me what is to be done, or even what should not be done, that pleases you. / I will fulfill your desire; you alone are my revered guru and beloved.
Speak your wish, my lord; I will carry it out according to my ability.' / When this was said, he replied to her: 'Why do you speak in vain, my dear?
You are not able, nor am I; it is useless to speak of it. / You are not qualified to ask about it, like a fruit on a very tall tree,
which a dwarf, standing on the ground, desires to reach. / In the same way, out of longing and infatuation for a woman, I desired what is unattainable.
I speak of a retreat that is difficult even for a married couple to achieve.' / The devoted wife said: / 'Once I understand what is in your mind, I am capable of accomplishing the task.
Give the command, my lord; it must be done by any means whatsoever! / If I can accomplish with effort this deed that is difficult for you to attain,
then great auspiciousness will bear fruit for me in the next world and here.' / When she said this, he stood up, exceedingly delighted, and spoke these words:
One who is accustomed to sin surely desires sin. / 'Seeing that exceedingly beautiful courtesan walking on this road,
flawless in every limb, my mind burns [with longing]. / If, by your grace, I could attain that youthful maiden,
then my life would be fruitful; O virtuous woman, bring about my welfare! / If that woman of shapely hips does not yield to me—a wretched leper,
foul-smelling and covered with fresh sores—then death would be better for me.' / Hearing the words he uttered, the virtuous wife said:
'I will do it to the best of my ability; now be at ease, my lord.' / Having considered it in her mind, at the end of the night, swiftly at dawn,
taking cow dung along with a broom, she went with joy. / Having reached the courtesan's house and cleaned the courtyard,
the street gateway, and the lane, she joyfully smeared them with cow dung. / She quickly returned to her house out of fear of being seen by people.
In this manner, that virtuous woman behaved for three days. / Then that chief courtesan asked her female and male servants:
'Whose splendid work is this in the courtyard? / Though I did not order it, who has done this at dawn for the sake of pleasing me?
The road, courtyard, and lanes are shining with charming work.' / Having deliberated among themselves, they said to the chief courtesan:
'This work of sweeping was not done by us, O good lady.' / Then, overcome with wonder, having reflected, at the end of the night
she saw that same woman who had come again just like before. / Seeing that great, virtuous, and devoted brahmin wife,
she held her feet, saying: 'Alas! Forgive me! / Life, body, prosperity, fame, wealth, and renown—
you seem to have appeared for the destruction of all these of mine, O devoted wife! / Whatever you ask, O virtuous woman, I will surely give it to you forever,
be it gold, gems, jewels, fine clothes, or whatever is your heart's desire.' / Then the virtuous wife said to her: 'I have no need of wealth.
There is a certain task for you; I will tell you, and if you do it, / then there will be satisfaction in my heart, and all will be accomplished by you now.'
The courtesan said: / 'Truly, truly I will do it! Speak quickly, O devoted wife! / Protect me, O mother, and tell me quickly what is to be done.'
Shamefully, the [virtuous wife] spoke what had to be said, stating the beloved boon of her husband. / Reflecting for a moment, that courtesan exercised forbearance and said:
'Though deeply grieved by union with a leper who smells foul, / I will do it for one day if he comes to my house.'
The devoted wife said: / 'I will come to your house tonight, O beautiful one; / having enjoyed his pleasure and being made glad, I will bring my husband back to my house.'
The courtesan said: / 'Go quickly to your house, O fortunate one, O devoted wife! / Let your husband come to my house at midnight.
I have many lovers, kings and their equals, / and one of them is always staying in my house without interruption.
Today, out of fear of you, I will make my house empty; / let your husband come, and having attained me, let him depart.'
Hearing this, the virtuous woman went to her own house / and announced to her husband: 'Your task has borne fruit, my lord!
She has agreed for you to go to her house tonight; / but she has many masters, so there is no time to lose.'
The brahmin said: / 'How will I go to her house? I am not able to walk. / Knowing this, where is the relief? How will the task be accomplished?'
The devoted wife said: / 'Placing you upon my own back, I will carry you to her house; / and when the purpose is accomplished, I will bring you back by that very path.'
The twice-born said: / 'O auspicious lady, only by your deed will my entire purpose be attained! / Now a deed has been performed by you that is unbearable even for womanhood.'
In that charming city, much wealth was constantly stolen by citizens from a rich man's house, / and the king then heard of it.
Having heard, the king angrily summoned all the night watchmen [and said]: / 'If you desire to live, you must deliver the thief to me today!'
Having received the king's order, anxious in their eagerness to seize him, / the spies forcefully captured a thief by the king's command.
Near the city, at the root of a tree in a dense forest, / the illustrious, eminent sage Māṇḍavya was absorbed in meditation (samādhi).
The foremost sage among yogins remained standing there like fire; / his breath had entered the inner channels, and nothing appeared [externally] to him.
Seeing that great sage standing equal to Brahman, the wicked men [said]: / 'This thief of strange appearance, a rogue, is standing in the forest!'
Having spoken thus, the wicked ones bound that best of sages; / and those excessively cruel men were neither spoken to nor looked at by him.
Then the king said this: "The thief has been caught by me. / Inflict terrible punishment [upon him] on the path near the gateway."
And the sage Māṇḍavya was impaled there upon a stake on the path; / the stake was driven by them into his anal region up to his head.
And he felt no pain, though his body was pierced on the stake, because of his restraint; / the punishment inflicted by others was made beneficial to his mind by them.
Meanwhile, at night in dense, rising darkness, / that devoted wife, having placed her husband on her back, departed.
From contact with Māṇḍavya's body, the smell of the leper reached him; / thus his meditation was truly broken through association with the leper.
Māṇḍavya said: 'He by whom this distress and bodily torment has just now been caused, / let that very person turn to ashes when the sun rises!'
Having been spoken to thus by Māṇḍavya, he fell onto the ground; / then the devoted wife also said: "Truly, may the sun not rise!"
Having taken [him] home for three days, having gone home from the curse, / the devoted wife remained, holding [him] lying on a lovely bed.
Having cursed him, the best of sages went to his desired region; / and the sun did not rise in the world for three days.
Seeing the entire threefold world with its moving and unmoving beings distressed, / the gods, placing Indra at their head, went to the Grandfather.
The denizens of heaven reported the entire occurrence to the lotus-born [Brahmā]: / "We do not know the cause; do you ordain what is fitting for us."
Brahmā said— / what happened with the devoted wife, and what happened with the sage Māṇḍavya, / and how the sun did not rise—the Creator explained among the gods.
Then the gods, in their aerial chariots, placing Prajāpati at their head, / went near to that place, O brāhmaṇa, and all [came] swiftly to the earth's surface.
By the splendour of those aerial chariots and likewise by the rays of the sages, / it shone as if with a hundred suns within that house and nowhere else.
"Alas, I am undone! How has the sun appeared in my house?" / Then she saw the gods with their aerial chariots resembling swans.
Meanwhile, Brahmā spoke to that devoted wife: / "Of all the gods, and of the twice-born, and of the cows likewise,
how is the destruction of these pleasing to you? / O mother, abandon your anger today regarding the rising of the sun."
The devoted wife said: / "Surpassing all worlds, my husband alone is my guru; / his death will occur from the sage's curse when the sun rises.
For that very reason this maker of day was cursed by me, / not out of wrath, nor delusion, nor greed, passion, or jealousy."
Brahmā said: / "By the death of one alone, the welfare of the three worlds would be achieved; / from that, O mother, even greater merit will accrue to you."
She said to the Ordainer there in front of the gods: / "Abandoning my husband, indeed, no auspiciousness pleases me."
Brahmā said: / "When the sun has risen, gentle lady, and your husband has been reduced to ashes, / and the threefold world has become healthy, I shall accomplish your welfare.
From the ashes a man will arise, equal in splendour to Kāmadeva, / a husband endowed with all virtues, and you [shall be] ever like Rati.
Just as Hari is worshipped by the gods, and just as Lakṣmī is worshipped, / so shall you two spouses be in heaven; therefore do my bidding."
The devoted wife said: / "Upon the death of my husband, O Brahmā, a widow blamed by the world, / into what worlds shall I go, fallen from conduct and defiled?"
Brahmā said: / "Therefore there is no fault in you; indeed, your husband is not dead now. / By our word alone, the leper shall attain the nature of Manmatha."
While the Ordainer was speaking thus, she reflected for a moment, / and she said, "Yes!"; thereupon the rising of the sun took place.
Tormented by the sage's curse, he turned into ashes; / from the midst of the ashes a twice-born was born, tormented by passion.
Seeing [this], all those city-dwellers were struck with wonder; / the hosts of gods were delighted, and the people became very comfortable.
In a sun-coloured aerial chariot that came from the heavenly realm, / along with her husband, that virtuous woman went to heaven together with the gods.
Since an auspicious devoted wife is thus equal even to me, / through that she knows what has occurred, the past, the future, and present activity.
Whoever recites this peerless, holy narrative in the world, / his sin committed across life after life goes to destruction.
He obtains imperishable heaven and is united with the wise; / a brāhmaṇa gains the Veda in birth after birth, O priest.
He who hears it once, purified, is freed from a flood of evil deeds; / he attains the abode of the gods, and fallen from heaven, becomes wealthy.
